data.name: Japanese Spinach Salad With Toasted Sesame Dressing
data.description: Tender, bright green spinach carries a nutty toasted-sesame dressing with savory soy sauce and gentle sweetness. Coarsely ground seeds give this cool Japanese salad a delicate, pleasantly grainy texture.

not_suitable_for: People with wheat allergies or celiac disease, because regular soy sauce contains wheat

refrigerator.notes: Refrigerate promptly in a covered container at 4°C (40°F) or below, within 2 hours of preparation. Best texture is on the day of preparation.

freezer.notes: Freezing is not recommended because the dressed spinach becomes watery after thawing.

storage.reheating: Serve cold from the refrigerator; reheating is unnecessary.

equipment.name: Mortar and pestle
equipment.alternative: Spice grinder, used in short pulses

items.name: spinach
items.notes: Edible weight of leaves and tender stems after removing roots and damaged leaves.

items.name: sesame seeds
items.notes: Toast gently and grind during preparation; all seeds are included in the dressing.

items.name: soy sauce
items.notes: Use regular Japanese soy sauce; weigh directly into the dressing.

items.name: water
items.notes: Plain water used only for blanching; discarded after cooking.

items.name: water
items.notes: Plain water used only to cool the spinach; discarded after cooling.

instructions.text: Bring the blanching water to a rolling boil in the large saucepan, approximately 100°C (212°F) at sea level.

doneness_cues.visual: Large bubbles continuously break across the water surface.

tips: Prepare the dressing while the water heats to keep the total preparation within 25 minutes.

instructions.text: Toast the sesame seeds in the dry skillet over medium-low heat for 2–3 minutes, stirring with the spoon until fragrant and lightly golden.

doneness_cues.visual: The seeds deepen slightly in color without developing dark patches.

tips: If the seeds are already toasted, warm them only briefly until fragrant.

instructions.text: Cool the toasted sesame seeds in the mortar for 2 minutes.
Crush the sesame seeds with the pestle until most are broken and the mixture resembles coarse, slightly oily sand.

doneness_cues.visual: Most seeds are ground, with a few small pieces remaining.

instructions.text: Mix the ground sesame seeds, soy sauce and sugar in the mixing bowl until evenly combined into a thick dressing.
Blanch the spinach in the boiling water for 45–60 seconds, submerging it with the tongs until the leaves wilt and the stems become tender but retain a slight bite.

doneness_cues.visual: Leaves are bright green and fully wilted.
doneness_cues.tactile: Tender stems bend easily but are not mushy.

instructions.text: Cool the spinach immediately in the large cooling bowl containing the cold cooling water, using the tongs to transfer it from the saucepan. Leave submerged for about 1 minute, until cool throughout.

doneness_cues.tactile: The leaves and stems no longer feel warm.

instructions.text: Drain the cooled spinach in the colander, discarding the cooling water and blanching water.
Squeeze the spinach gently in small handfuls with clean hands until water stops dripping steadily.

doneness_cues.tactile: The spinach remains moist and supple without releasing a stream of water.

instructions.text: Cut the squeezed spinach into approximately 4 cm lengths on the cutting board using the knife.
Toss the spinach with the dressing in the mixing bowl, separating compacted clumps with the tongs until the leaves are evenly coated.

doneness_cues.visual: Sesame dressing clings evenly to the spinach with no watery pool underneath.

instructions.text: Divide the salad evenly among four serving bowls.

troubleshooting.symptom: The dressing becomes watery and slides off the spinach.
troubleshooting.likely_cause: Too much cooling water remains trapped between the leaves.
troubleshooting.prevention: Squeeze the cooled spinach in small handfuls before cutting and dressing.
troubleshooting.fix: Drain any pooled liquid and gently toss again. Avoid squeezing dressed spinach, which removes the sesame dressing.

troubleshooting.likely_cause: The sesame seeds scorched during toasting.
troubleshooting.prevention: Use medium-low heat, stir frequently and remove the seeds as soon as they smell nutty.
troubleshooting.fix: Discard the burnt seeds or dressing and remake the dressing before combining it with the spinach.

chef_notes: Grinding the sesame seeds releases their oils and helps the dressing cling to the spinach; leaving every seed whole produces a looser coating.
A coarse grind preserves a little texture without requiring added sesame oil.
Keep the tender spinach stems because they provide a pleasant contrast to the soft leaves.
Dress the spinach shortly before serving for the freshest texture.
Finished weight depends on how much water is squeezed from the spinach; weigh the completed salad and divide by four if a measured serving weight is needed.
data.cultural_context: Goma-ae refers to Japanese dishes dressed with ground sesame, and spinach is a familiar example. The preparation also suits other blanched vegetables, including green beans, as described in [Just One Cookbook](https://www.justonecookbook.com/spinach-with-sesame-sauce/).
